name: Staff and platform impersonation
description: Accounts claiming to be VRChat staff, group moderators, or verified accounts when they are not. This is how most social-engineering attacks on these communities begin -- a fake moderator asking a member to 'verify' something. Scoped mostly to display names and status, because that is where the claim has to appear to work.

rules.note: Claiming to be VRChat itself. VRChat staff do not moderate individual group instances and do not contact users through profiles. Note the false positive: a genuine VRChat employee may well be in your group as a member, and some list it in their bio honestly. Check before acting -- a real one will not mind being asked.

Authority claims in the nameplate. Scoped to displayName and status because the claim only works where it is seen first. Bios are excluded -- a bio saying 'official account of our group' is often simply true. Verify against your group roster; that check takes ten seconds and settles it.

Verification-badge characters in a display name -- check marks, the blue diamond, the ballot-box tick. Used to fake the visual language of a verified account. Plenty of people also just like tick emoji, so this is review and display-name-scoped. Look at whether the rest of the name makes an authority claim.

Claiming a staff role AND soliciting reports, which is the combination that actually causes harm -- it redirects members away from real staff at the moment they most need them. Role words alone are far too common (everyone is a mod of something) which is why the solicitation half is required.
Credential phishing wearing a staff uniform. No legitimate verification flow starts from a stranger's profile. This is the payload that the rest of the rules in this list are the setup for.

Impersonating this tool. A moderation bot's name carries authority precisely because members are told to trust it, which makes it worth stealing. Modbot does not DM members and does not ask for anything.

Identity disputes between two accounts claiming to be the same person. Usually means one account is impersonating another, and occasionally means a member has been locked out of their own. The flag tells you to look at both; it does not tell you which is which.

Cyrillic letters that render identically to Latin ones -- а, е, о, р, с, х and friends -- used to register a display name that looks exactly like an existing member's or a staff account's. Normalisation and confusable folding should already collapse these before matching, so a hit on this rule usually means the raw name is being checked deliberately. Obvious and important false positive: members who actually write in Russian, Ukrainian, Serbian or Bulgarian. Look at whether the whole name is Cyrillic (fine) or just two letters in an otherwise Latin name (not fine).

Fake appeals handling. Targets members who are already banned or worried about being banned, and therefore already anxious and less likely to check. If your group has a real appeals process, say where it is publicly -- that does more than this rule does.

Recorded. Accounts styling themselves as the official arm of something. Frequently harmless branding by a member who runs a fan community, which is why it only records. Useful when a group is being actively impersonated and you need to find the copies.
